concepts.title: Walkthrough: Designing a URL Shortener
concepts.description: A URL shortener is small enough to fit in one head, but it forces the same three decisions that show up in far larger systems: how to generate IDs, how read-heavy the workload is, and where caching pays for itself. That's why it's the canonical first system-design walkthrough.
learningObjectives: Compare three ID-generation strategies for short codes (random-with-retry, counter-plus-encoding, pre-generated key pools) and explain the failure mode each one avoids or introduces.
Explain why a URL shortener's read/write ratio is one of the most skewed you'll encounter, and derive the caching strategy that follows directly from it.
Apply the cache-aside pattern with a long TTL to the specific redirect-lookup access pattern and justify why this pattern fits better than write-through here.
Explain the tradeoff between 301 and 302 redirects in terms of caching, server load, and analytics visibility.
Identify why click-analytics logging must be kept off the hot redirect path and describe how to decouple it.

sections.heading: Framing the Problem Before Reaching for Any Tool
sections.body:
The requirements, stripped down: a user submits a long URL and gets back a short code (`https://short.ly/aZ9k2`); visiting the short URL redirects to the original. Add a few realistic extras (custom aliases, an optional expiration date, basic click analytics) and you have the whole problem. It's small on purpose, which is its value as a study problem: every design decision below is forced by the requirements, not by arbitrary scale assumptions, and the same three decisions (how to generate unique keys, what the read/write ratio is, where caching pays for itself) recur in systems with far more moving parts.

Don't treat it as trivial because the feature description is short. A shortener that just base64-encodes the long URL doesn't produce short codes at all (the encoding is longer than the input), and it ignores every scaling question that makes this a useful exercise.

sections.heading: ID Generation: The First Design Decision
sections.body:
There are three common approaches, and the differences matter well before serious scale. **Random string plus collision check**: generate a random 6-7 character string, check whether it's taken, and retry on collision. It's simple and needs no coordination between servers, but every write costs at least one extra database read (the collision check) before the insert, and the collision probability, low for a well-chosen character set and length, rises as the keyspace fills, so retries become more frequent as the system grows.

**Auto-incrementing counter, base62-encoded**: take a strictly increasing integer ID (1, 2, 3, ...) and encode it in base62 (`[a-zA-Z0-9]`, 62 characters) to get a short, unique code with no collision checks. It's elegant and cheap per write, but a single global counter is a point of write contention, the kind of shared, unscalable bottleneck the database-scaling module warned about, and sequential codes are trivially enumerable (`short.ly/1`, `short.ly/2`, ...), which leaks creation order and volume and lets anyone scrape every shortened URL by counting.

**Pre-generated key pools**: a background worker generates batches of random, guaranteed-unique keys ahead of time and stores them in a "not yet used" pool; each creation request pops one off instead of generating or checking anything inline. Key generation leaves the request path: the expensive part (ensuring uniqueness) happens asynchronously, in bulk, and avoids both the retry cost of the random approach and the contention of the single counter. Large shorteners tend to use this approach because it removes coordination from the write path instead of trying to make it faster. To keep the pool itself from becoming a hot spot, each app server can claim a batch of keys (say 1,000) at a time and hand them out locally. Custom aliases are a separate case: a user-chosen alias still needs a uniqueness check, usually a unique index on `short_code` and a "409 conflict, alias taken" response, since it can't come from the pool.

sections.heading: The Read/Write Ratio Changes Everything About the Architecture
sections.body:
A URL shortener is one of the most read-skewed systems you'll design: a URL is created once and then clicked thousands or millions of times over its lifetime, especially if it goes viral. Realistic estimates put the read-to-write ratio at 100:1 or higher, unlike a social feed or e-commerce catalog with more balanced traffic. That one fact should dominate the rest of the design: the system doesn't need to be optimized for write throughput (writes are rare and individually cheap), it needs to serve an enormous volume of redirect lookups as fast and cheaply as possible.

That is the profile the caching module described as the best case for aggressive caching: the `short_code -> long_url` mapping is close to immutable once created (barring an edit feature or expiration), access is heavily skewed toward a small hot set of popular links at any moment, and a cache hit avoids a database round trip on the dominant type of request. Caching isn't a nice-to-have here. Given how lopsided the ratio is, it's the highest-leverage decision in the design. A quick sizing check shows why storage isn't the worry: 100 creates/sec is 8.64 million a day, or about 3.15 billion a year, and at roughly 500 bytes per row (code, URL, timestamps, metadata) that is about 1.6 TB a year. That's large but ordinary for one sharded or managed store, while the 10,000 reads/sec are what need the cache.

sections.heading: Where the Data Lives, and the 301 vs. 302 Tradeoff
sections.body:
The core data model is about as simple as a mapping gets, `short_code -> long_url` plus metadata like creation time and optional expiration. It fits a relational table with an index on `short_code` or a key-value store, and either is defensible, since the access pattern (point lookups by exact key, no joins) doesn't demand a particular database family. If write volume or row count outgrows one machine, which is unlikely for most deployments of this feature, sharding by `hash(short_code)` is the natural lever, reusing the shard-key reasoning from the database-scaling module: hashing the lookup key distributes load evenly and matches the dominant query, since every read is already keyed by `short_code`.

A product-level tradeoff hides in the choice between an HTTP 301 (permanent redirect) and a 302 (temporary redirect). A 301 tells browsers "cache this redirect, don't ask again," so repeat visits from the same browser never reach the server after the first one. That's excellent for load, but the server loses visibility into those clicks, because the browser satisfies them locally. A 302 tells the browser "this might change, check every time," which keeps every click visible to the server (valuable if click analytics matter) at the cost of never letting browsers cache the redirect. Neither is objectively correct; it's a business decision about whether click-tracking accuracy or load reduction matters more for the product.

sections.heading: Click Analytics: A Separate, Asynchronous Write Path
sections.body:
The redirect itself, looking up `short_code` and responding with a redirect to `long_url`, has to stay on the fastest possible path, since it runs on nearly every request. Recording analytics about the click (timestamp, referrer, rough geography, user agent) is a different concern with a different latency requirement: nobody is waiting on the analytics write the way a user is waiting on the redirect, so it must not slow the redirect down or, worse, fail it if the analytics write has a transient problem.

The fix is to decouple the two paths. The redirect handler does its cache or database lookup and responds immediately, while the analytics event is recorded asynchronously (put on a queue or logged in a way that doesn't block the response) and processed later by whatever system aggregates click statistics. A common setup logs click events to a queue or log stream and aggregates them in batches, which is fine because per-link click counts can be eventually consistent: nobody is hurt if a dashboard lags by a minute. It's the same separation-of-concerns instinct that appears throughout system design: keep the path a user is waiting on short and failure-resistant, and push everything not required to produce that response onto a path with a more forgiving latency and failure budget.

examples.title: Base62 Encoding a Counter-Generated ID
examples.code:
ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789"
BASE = len(ALPHABET)  # 62

def encode_base62(n):
    if n == 0:
        return ALPHABET[0]
    chars = []
    while n > 0:
        n, remainder = divmod(n, BASE)
        chars.append(ALPHABET[remainder])
    return "".join(reversed(chars))

# a counter (e.g. an auto-increment DB column) hands out strictly
# increasing integers -- no collision check is ever needed
print(encode_base62(1))          # 'b'
print(encode_base62(125))        # 'cb'
print(encode_base62(3521614606208))  # 8 characters -- 62^8 is over 218 trillion codes
examples.explanation: Because the database guarantees the underlying integer is unique, encoding it in base62 gives a unique short code with no collision checks and no retries, a real efficiency gain over random-with-retry. The cost, visible in the output, is that codes are sequential and predictable: anyone can infer that 'cb' was the 125th URL ever created, and can enumerate every issued code by counting up from 1, which leaks creation volume and approximate order in a way a random or pre-generated key wouldn't. Real systems either accept that as a non-issue for their use case, add a permutation or obfuscation step on top of the counter, or move to a pre-generated random key pool. For sizing, 62^6 is about 56.8 billion codes and 62^7 about 3.5 trillion, so 7 characters is plenty for most services.

examples.title: Cache-Aside Redirect Handler, With and Without the Cache
examples.explanation: With a 100:1 or higher read-to-write ratio, the naive version sends nearly every read to the database, so the database has to be provisioned for the full redirect volume of the whole system even though the data barely changes. The cached version, with a realistic hit rate for this pattern (very high, since the mapping is nearly immutable and access skews toward popular links), removes most of that traffic from the database, which sees only cache misses and the much smaller write volume. The 24-hour TTL is long because this data almost never changes after creation. If links can expire, the cache TTL must never outlive the link: set it to the smaller of 24 hours and the time remaining until expiry, or an expired link keeps redirecting from the cache. It would be wrong for a price or an inventory count, but the caching module's core question, how tolerant the data is of staleness and how often it changes, has a favorable answer here.

examples.title: Why Caching Is the Highest-Leverage Decision: A Back-of-Envelope Comparison
examples.code:
Assumptions for a moderately popular shortener:
  Writes (new short URLs created): 100/sec
  Reads (redirects served):      10,000/sec
  Read/write ratio: 100:1

WITHOUT a cache:
  Database must sustain ~10,100 queries/sec (10,000 reads + 100 writes)
  -- almost entirely driven by the read volume

WITH a cache at a realistic 95% hit rate for this access pattern:
  Database sees: 100 writes/sec + (10,000 * 0.05) cache-miss reads/sec
               = 100 + 500 = 600 queries/sec
  -- roughly a 94% reduction in total database load, letting a single,
     modestly-sized database instance handle traffic that would
     otherwise have required serious read-replica scaling
examples.explanation: This mirrors the diagnostic exercise from the caching module: database load without a cache is dominated by reads, because they outnumber writes by two orders of magnitude. A 95% hit rate, well within reach for a mapping this stable and skewed, removes most of the read load, cutting required database capacity from 10,100 to 600 queries/sec, a reduction of about 94%, or 17x. That is the numeric version of the claim that caching is the highest-leverage decision in this design: not a tuning improvement, but the difference between a scaled-out read-replica fleet and a single modest database instance.

misconceptions.description: A URL shortener is such a 'simple' feature (it's just a redirect) that it doesn't really need any serious system-design thought.
misconceptions.clarification: The feature description is short, but it forces the same three decisions found in far more complex systems: how to generate unique identifiers without a coordination bottleneck, what the read/write ratio implies about where to spend engineering effort, and which caching pattern and invalidation policy fit this data's staleness tolerance. That's why it's a canonical study problem: its small size lets those decisions show up cleanly, without unrelated complexity in the way.

misconceptions.description: A single auto-incrementing counter in the database is a perfectly fine way to generate short codes, since URL-creation writes are relatively rare compared to redirects.
misconceptions.clarification: Writes being rare compared to reads doesn't make a single global counter free of problems. Every server generating a code has to coordinate through that one counter, the shared, unscalable write bottleneck described in the database-scaling module, and it becomes a contention point as write volume grows even if writes stay a small fraction of traffic. There's also a non-performance cost: sequential codes are trivially enumerable, so anyone can infer creation volume and order or scrape every issued code by counting upward. A pre-generated pool of random keys avoids both problems by moving uniqueness checking off the request path and keeping codes non-sequential.

exercises.prompt: A URL shortener sees 200 creates/sec and 20,000 redirects/sec. Compute the total database query load in two scenarios: (a) no caching at all, and (b) cache-aside with a 98% hit rate on redirect lookups. Predict roughly how much smaller the database's required capacity is in scenario (b), and explain why write load is barely relevant to that comparison.
exercises.code:
Writes (creates): 200/sec
Reads (redirects): 20,000/sec

Scenario (a): no cache -- every redirect hits the database directly
Scenario (b): cache-aside, 98% hit rate on redirect lookups
hints: In scenario (a), total database load is just writes plus ALL reads -- there's no cache to absorb any of them.
In scenario (b), only the 2% of reads that MISS the cache actually reach the database -- compute 20,000 * 0.02.
Add the (much smaller) missed-read count to the write count in scenario (b), then compare that total to scenario (a)'s total to see the ratio.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Scenario (a): 200 + 20,000 = 20,200 queries/sec hit the database. Scenario (b): 200 writes/sec + (20,000 * 0.02) = 200 + 400 = 600 queries/sec. That's a reduction of about 34x (20,200 down to 600; 20,200 / 600 = 33.7), driven by the cache absorbing 98% of the read traffic. Writes stay at 200/sec in both scenarios, because caching this mapping does nothing to write volume; it only reduces how many reads reach the database.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The comparison is dominated by the read side because reads (20,000/sec) outnumber writes (200/sec) 100:1 to begin with, the skew typical of a URL shortener. Caching filters the read path only. The 200 writes/sec pass through unchanged in both scenarios, while 98% of reads never reach the database in scenario (b), leaving the 2% miss rate (400/sec) to add to the unchanged writes. The roughly 34x drop in database load is the numeric payoff of matching the caching strategy to the workload's read skew, and it shows why effort on the caching layer buys far more capacity than any write-path optimization would: writes were never the bottleneck.

exercises.prompt: A URL shortener's redirect handler is slow under load and occasionally fails redirects entirely. Investigation shows it performs the redirect lookup AND writes a click-analytics row to the database, synchronously, in the same request, before responding. During a brief spike in analytics-table write latency, redirect responses slow down or time out even though the actual short_code -> long_url lookup itself is fast. Diagnose the problem and fix it.
hints: The actual short_code lookup is fast (helped by the cache) -- so what specifically is adding latency and occasional failures to the response?
Does the user waiting for their redirect care at all whether the click-analytics row has been written yet, or is that purely a backend bookkeeping concern?
The fix is about WHEN the analytics write happens relative to the response, not about making the analytics write itself faster.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The handler bundles two operations with very different latency and reliability needs into one synchronous request: the redirect lookup, which the user is waiting on, and the analytics write, which is backend bookkeeping the user has no stake in finishing before the response arrives. Because both are on the same path, slowness or a transient failure in the analytics table, which has nothing to do with the redirect's health, degrades or breaks the redirect, which is what was observed. The fix decouples them: the redirect responds as soon as it has the long URL (fast, cache-assisted, and now the only thing gating the response), while the analytics event is handed to a queue or other asynchronous mechanism that processes it on its own schedule with its own failure handling. A slow or failing analytics pipeline can no longer touch the redirect path. The tradeoff is that a click event can be lost if the enqueue itself fails; for analytics that is usually acceptable, and it would not be for billing.

assessments.prompt: Which caching pattern and TTL choice best fits the short_code -> long_url redirect lookup in a URL shortener, and why?
options: Write-through caching with a 5-second TTL, because the data changes frequently and must always be immediately fresh.
Cache-aside with a long TTL, because the mapping almost never changes and access is heavily read-skewed.
Write-back (write-behind) caching, because redirect lookups are the write-heavy part of this workload.
No caching at all, because database reads on an indexed short_code column are already fast enough on their own.
assessments.explanation: Cache-aside with a long TTL matches this data: the mapping almost never changes after creation, so a long TTL carries negligible staleness risk, and access is skewed toward a hot subset of popular links, which cache-aside handles well because it caches only what has been requested. The “Write-through caching with a 5-second TTL…” option is wrong on both counts: the data isn't frequently changing, and a 5-second TTL would defeat almost all of the caching benefit, sending most redirects to the database anyway. The “No caching at all, because database reads…” option ignores the read/write ratio: at 100:1 or higher, even a fast indexed query multiplied by the full read volume is far more database load than the same traffic after a high hit rate. The “Write-back (write-behind) caching, because redirect lookups…” option misreads the workload: redirects are the read side, and write-back addresses fast, loss-tolerant writes, which aren't the bottleneck here.

assessments.prompt: Walk through the end-to-end design of a URL shortener, explaining how ID generation, the read/write ratio, and caching strategy connect and reinforce each other as one coherent design instead of three unrelated decisions.
assessments.modelAnswer: The three decisions aren't independent: each is shaped by the others, starting from one fact about this workload. Redirects vastly outnumber creations, often 100:1 or more, because a single short URL can be clicked far more times than it was created. That read/write skew comes first because it tells you where effort pays off: optimizing the write path (ID generation) matters for correctness and avoiding contention, but the capacity win is in the read path, since reads are nearly all the traffic. For ID generation I'd lean toward a pre-generated pool of random keys over a single auto-incrementing counter: the counter is simple and collision-free, but it creates a point of write contention that doesn't need to exist when writes are already rare relative to reads, and its sequential codes leak creation order and volume. A pre-generated pool takes the expensive part (guaranteeing uniqueness) off the request path by generating batches of keys asynchronously ahead of time, so each creation request pops a ready-made key with no inline coordination. For the read path, the short_code-to-long_url mapping is essentially immutable once created and access skews toward a hot subset of popular links, so cache-aside with a long TTL fits: the application checks the cache first, falls back to the database only on a miss, and a TTL of hours or more adds minimal staleness risk because this data rarely changes. The payoff compounds with the read skew: reads dominate by two orders of magnitude and the cache can plausibly absorb 95% or more of them, so the load reaching the database drops to roughly the write volume plus a small trickle of misses, letting a modest database handle traffic that would otherwise need serious read-replica scaling. Finally, click analytics stay off this hot path and are recorded asynchronously, so a slow or failing analytics write can never degrade the redirect a user is waiting on. That reinforces the principle behind the caching decision: keep the path most requests take fast and failure-isolated, and push everything non-essential to that response onto a separate path with its own, more forgiving budget.

assessments.prompt: Why recommend a pre-generated pool of random keys over a single auto-incrementing counter for short codes, even though writes are comparatively rare in this system?
options: Because auto-incrementing counters cannot be encoded in base62 under any circumstances.
Because random keys are always shorter than base62-encoded counter values.
Because pre-generated key pools are the only approach that supports custom aliases.

Because a single global counter is still a shared, unscalable point of write contention regardless of how rare writes are relative to reads, and sequential codes are trivially enumerable, letting anyone scrape every issued short code just by counting -- a pre-generated pool avoids both problems by moving uniqueness-checking off the request path entirely.
assessments.explanation: Relative rarity of writes doesn't make a single global counter free of problems: it becomes a contention point as write volume grows even if writes stay a small fraction of traffic, and its sequential codes are trivially enumerable, letting anyone infer creation volume and order or scrape every issued code by counting upward. A pre-generated pool avoids both by moving uniqueness checking off the request path. The “Because auto-incrementing counters cannot be encoded…” option is false: the encoding example shows a counter being base62-encoded. The “Because pre-generated key pools are the only…” option invents a claim about custom aliases. The “Because random keys are always shorter…” option makes an unsupported length comparison.

assessments.prompt: A product team debating 301 vs. 302 redirects for their URL shortener wants click analytics on every visit to a short link, including repeat visits from the same browser. Which status code should they use, and what do they give up?
options: 301, because permanent redirects are always the technically correct choice for a URL shortener.
301, because it makes the server aware of every single click including repeat visits from the same browser.

302, because it tells the browser to check with the server every time rather than caching the redirect locally, keeping every click visible to the server -- at the cost of never letting browsers cache the redirect away, which increases server load compared to 301.
Neither -- click analytics require a completely different HTTP status code that doesn't yet exist in the standard.
assessments.explanation: A 302 keeps every click visible to the server, at the cost of never letting browsers cache the redirect, while a 301 means repeat visits from the same browser never reach the server after the first, so the server loses visibility into those clicks. The “301, because permanent redirects are always…” and “301, because it makes the server aware…” options both claim 301 preserves click visibility, which is the opposite of what happens. The “Neither -- click analytics require a completely…” option invents a nonexistent status code requirement.

assessments.prompt: What goes wrong if the analytics write happens synchronously, in the same request, before the redirect response is sent?
options: A slowdown or transient failure in the analytics write directly delays or breaks the redirect response.
The redirect would be sent to the wrong long_url as a direct result of the analytics write occurring first.
Synchronous analytics writes make the short_code lookup itself impossible to cache.
Nothing goes wrong -- synchronous analytics writes are described as the recommended default for this system.
assessments.explanation: Analytics recording must not slow the redirect down or fail it if the analytics write has a transient problem, because nobody is waiting on the analytics write the way a user is waiting on the redirect. The “Nothing goes wrong -- synchronous analytics writes…” option contradicts the recommendation to decouple the two paths. The “The redirect would be sent…” option invents a data-correctness problem with no causal link. The “Synchronous analytics writes make the short_code lookup…” option fabricates a caching impossibility.

assessments.prompt: If a URL shortener's write volume or total row count outgrows a single machine, sharding by hash(short_code) is the natural choice. Why does this shard key work well here, using the reasoning from the database-scaling module?
options: Because hashing the lookup key itself distributes load evenly across shards and matches the dominant query pattern exactly, since every redirect read is already keyed by short_code.
Because short_code values are numeric, and only numeric fields can be used as shard keys.
Because hash(short_code) guarantees that no caching layer is ever needed once sharding is in place, since every shard can keep its complete share of the mapping in memory at all times.
Because hashing short_code is the only shard key that any database technology supports.
assessments.explanation: Sharding by hash(short_code) reuses the shard-key reasoning from the database-scaling module: hashing the lookup key distributes load evenly and matches the dominant query, since every read is already keyed by short_code. The “Because hashing short_code is the only shard…” option fabricates a database restriction. The “Because hash(short_code) guarantees that no caching layer…” option is false: sharding and caching are separate, complementary concerns. The “Because short_code values are numeric, and only…” option is wrong on both counts: short_code is an alphanumeric base62 string, and shard keys don't have to be numeric.

concepts.title: Walkthrough: Designing a Basic Chat System
concepts.description: A chat system looks like "a CRUD API with WebSockets instead of HTTP," but connection handling, delivery guarantees, and message ordering make it a different problem shape, one where the statelessness and consistency assumptions from earlier modules have to be reconsidered, not just reused.
learningObjectives: Explain why a chat system's long-lived, bidirectional connections are a fundamentally different traffic shape than the stateless request/response model most of the earlier modules assumed.
Describe how a connection registry lets a stateful pool of connection servers route a message to whichever server currently holds a given user's socket.
Compare at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once delivery guarantees, and explain why practical systems approximate exactly-once with at-least-once plus client-side deduplication.
Explain store-and-forward delivery and why it's necessary for offline recipients.
Explain what ordering guarantee a chat conversation actually needs, and connect that requirement back to the consistency-tradeoffs concept.

sections.heading: Why This Is a Different Shape of Problem
sections.body:
Every system walked through so far in this subject, including the URL shortener in the previous lesson, shares one assumption: a client sends a request, a stateless server handles it using only the request's contents (plus data it can fetch from a shared store), and sends back a response. That model is what let load balancers route freely and horizontal scaling work cleanly, as covered in the load-balancing and statelessness lesson.

A chat system breaks that assumption at its foundation. A user needs to *receive* messages the server initiates at any moment, without having asked for them, so there's no "request" for an incoming message to be the response to. That requires a long-lived, open, bidirectional connection between the client and some specific server for as long as the user is online. The moment that connection exists, it is state tied to one machine, the kind of state the earlier modules worked to design *away* from. Chat isn't a CRUD API with a different transport. It reintroduces the statefulness the rest of this subject spent effort eliminating, and the design has to manage that state on purpose.

sections.heading: Connection Handling at Scale: WebSockets and the Return of State
sections.body:
A **WebSocket** (or a similar persistent-connection technology) keeps a single TCP connection open between a client and a specific server for as long as the user is connected, letting either side send data at any time without a new request/response round trip. Each open connection uses ongoing resources on the server holding it (memory for connection state, a file descriptor, some share of the machine's connection-handling capacity), so scaling to millions of concurrent users means a horizontally scaled pool of **connection servers**, each holding a slice of the connected population. As an illustration, if one server can hold about 100,000 mostly idle connections (a figure that depends heavily on memory per connection and tuning), 10 million concurrent users need at least 100 connection servers, plus headroom for failures.

That creates a specific problem. If user A is connected to connection-server 7, and user B, connected to connection-server 3, sends A a message, server 3 has no way of knowing that server 7 holds A's socket. This is the load-balancing-and-statelessness problem again ("which instance is serving this user"), but it can't be solved by externalizing the data to a shared store the way a shopping cart was, because the open TCP socket itself, not just associated data, is pinned to one machine's memory and can't be moved. The standard fix is a **connection registry**: a shared, fast lookup service (commonly Redis) mapping `user_id -> which connection server holds their socket`, updated on every connect and disconnect, with an expiry refreshed by a periodic heartbeat so that a crashed server's users don't stay mapped to it forever. Any server that needs to deliver a message to A looks up the registry, finds server 7, and forwards the message internally (via an internal pub/sub channel or direct RPC) to server 7, the only one that can push it down A's live socket.

sections.heading: Message Delivery: Getting It There, and Knowing Whether It Got There
sections.body:
Delivery guarantees form a spectrum, and a chat system needs to sit at a particular point on it. **At-most-once** delivery sends a message and doesn't retry on failure. It's simple, but messages can vanish if a send fails, which is unacceptable in a chat product (a message the user typed and sent shouldn't just disappear). **At-least-once** delivery retries until it gets confirmation, so the message eventually arrives, but retries can deliver it more than once if an earlier acknowledgment was lost in transit (the message arrived, the ack didn't make it back, and the sender retries a message that already succeeded). **Exactly-once** delivery, one arrival with no duplicates and no losses, is what everyone wants intuitively, but over an unreliable network where messages and acknowledgments can both be delayed or lost independently it's provably hard, and most real systems don't implement it at the transport level.

What real chat systems do is combine **at-least-once delivery** with **client-side deduplication**: every message gets a unique ID, generated by the sending client so it stays stable across retries, and the receiving client (or the server, before persisting) discards any message whose ID it has already seen. The user gets the experience of exactly-once, since they never see a duplicate, while the underlying mechanism only has to solve the more tractable at-least-once problem, with the small remaining task (recognizing and dropping a duplicate) pushed to whichever side can do it cheaply.

sections.heading: Handling Offline Recipients: Store-and-Forward
sections.body:
Live delivery over an open connection only works if the recipient has an open connection right now, which for any real messaging product is often not true: people close laptops, lose signal, or aren't in the app. The pattern that handles this is **store-and-forward**: when a message is sent, it is first durably persisted to a message store (a database, keyed by conversation and sequence), and *only then* does the system attempt live delivery to the recipient's connection server, if one exists. If the recipient is offline, the durable write already succeeded, so no message is lost; it's waiting.

When the recipient reconnects, their client doesn't rely on having caught some one-time push. It asks the server for "everything in this conversation since the last message I have," which the durable store can answer reliably however long the client was offline or however many connection servers have come and gone. That reframes delivery as a durability-plus-catch-up problem instead of purely a live-push problem: the push over an open WebSocket is a fast-path optimization for when the recipient is online, layered on a durable store that is the source of truth and the actual guarantee.

sections.heading: Ordering, Consistency, and Putting the Whole Thing Together
sections.body:
Two participants in a conversation need to see messages in the same order: if A sends "are you free tomorrow" and then "never mind, I am", both A and B must see them in that order. This is done with a **per-conversation sequence number** (or a tightly scoped, monotonically increasing timestamp with a tie-breaker), assigned when a message is durably stored and used to order what's displayed. Note what this *doesn't* require: a single global ordering across every conversation in the system, which would demand the expensive, coordinated, strongly consistent write path across a heavily sharded system that the consistency-tradeoffs lesson warned against reaching for by default. What's needed is a narrower guarantee, read-your-own-writes and monotonic ordering *within one conversation*, matched to what users would notice being wrong: the "match, don't maximize" principle from that lesson. Sequence numbers need a single writer per conversation to be gap-free and contention-free, which is why messages are usually partitioned by conversation ID, the same idea as choosing a shard key that matches the query. Group chats extend the design naturally: the message is stored once in the conversation, and live delivery fans out to each member's connection server through the registry.

The full picture: a load balancer and gateway handle the connection handshake and authentication; a horizontally scaled pool of stateful connection servers each hold a slice of open sockets; a connection registry (shared, fast, externally visible) tracks which server holds which user's connection, which is what makes cross-server delivery possible; a durable message store persists every message first and serves both live-delivery lookups and reconnect catch-up queries; and per-conversation sequence numbers keep each conversation's ordering consistent for its participants. Adding more stateless replicas behind a load balancer doesn't solve the core new problem, which is which specific machine holds which specific open socket. That's why chat needed its own treatment of state instead of the statelessness playbook used elsewhere in this subject.

examples.title: Connection Registry: Routing a Message Across Connection Servers
examples.code:
User A connects -> load balancer assigns the WebSocket to connection-server-7
  connection-server-7: registry.set("conn:userA", "connection-server-7")

User B connects -> load balancer assigns the WebSocket to connection-server-3
  connection-server-3: registry.set("conn:userB", "connection-server-3")

User B sends a message to User A:
  1. connection-server-3 receives the message over B's socket
  2. connection-server-3 persists it to the durable message store (see next example)
  3. connection-server-3 looks up: registry.get("conn:userA") -> "connection-server-7"
  4. connection-server-3 forwards the message internally to connection-server-7
     (via internal pub/sub or direct RPC -- NOT back through the public load balancer)
  5. connection-server-7 pushes the message down A's actual open socket
examples.explanation: This is what makes cross-server delivery possible. connection-server-3 received the outbound message from B but has no socket to A and never will: A's socket lives in connection-server-7's process. The registry turns "deliver this to user A" into "find out which machine can do that, then ask it to." It's structurally the same fix as the shopping-cart example from the load-balancing lesson (move state pinned to one instance's memory into a shared, externally visible store), except that the registry doesn't hold the state itself, since the socket can't be moved into Redis. It holds a pointer to which instance does, which is how that idea adapts when the state can't be externalized directly.

examples.title: Store-and-Forward: Durability Before Delivery
examples.explanation: The ordering of operations is the point: durability happens first and unconditionally, and live delivery is attempted afterward as a best-effort optimization on top of a guarantee that doesn't depend on it. If `deliver_live` fails or the recipient has no connection server (fully offline), nothing is lost: the message already exists in `message_store`, and `sync_on_reconnect` lets the recipient's client catch up on what it missed by sequence number, without depending on any particular connection server having stayed alive. That makes store-and-forward robust to connection-server churn (restarts during deploys, crashes, scaling up or down), which a design relying purely on live push could never be.

examples.title: At-Least-Once Delivery Plus Client-Side Deduplication
examples.code:
Sender's client generates a stable ID for the message BEFORE sending:
  client_message_id = "a1b2c3"  (generated once, reused on every retry)

Attempt 1: client sends {id: "a1b2c3", text: "..."} -> server persists it,
           sends ack back -> ack is LOST in transit (network blip)
Attempt 2: client, having seen no ack, retries the SAME message
           {id: "a1b2c3", text: "..."} -> server checks: "a1b2c3" already
           persisted -> does NOT create a duplicate row, just re-sends the ack

Result: message persisted exactly once, despite being SENT twice --
        because deduplication happens by client-generated id, not by
        'did I receive a send request', which would have double-counted it
examples.explanation: This is the practical resolution of the exactly-once problem. Attempt 2 is a retry caused by a lost acknowledgment, not a new message, and the server can tell only because the client attached the same stable ID both times, generated once before the first send so retries carry it unchanged. If the server generated a fresh ID on each receipt, or the ID were omitted, the server couldn't recognize attempt 2 as a duplicate of attempt 1, and the recipient would see the message twice. The user-visible result, the message appearing once, comes from at-least-once delivery (the retry) plus cheap ID-based deduplication, with neither side implementing true distributed exactly-once semantics at the transport level.

misconceptions.description: A chat backend is essentially a CRUD API with a 'messages' table, just using WebSockets instead of HTTP for the transport.
misconceptions.clarification: The data model (a messages table) is the easy part and looks like plenty of ordinary CRUD features. The hard parts don't show up in a schema diagram: tracking which server instance holds which user's live connection (and routing cross-server messages through that registry), choosing a delivery guarantee that survives retries and lost acknowledgments without duplicating or losing messages, and handling offline recipients with durable store-and-forward instead of assuming a live push will land. Even features like "delivered" and "read" receipts reuse the same machinery: they are small messages flowing back through the registry and the store. None of that comes from the transport being WebSockets instead of HTTP. It comes from the traffic being long-lived, bidirectional, and server-initiated, which breaks the stateless request/response assumptions most CRUD APIs, and most earlier modules in this subject, get to rely on.

misconceptions.description: A well-engineered chat system should implement true exactly-once message delivery, since duplicate or lost messages are both unacceptable.
misconceptions.clarification: True exactly-once delivery at the transport level, over a network where messages and their acknowledgments can independently be delayed or lost, is famously difficult and largely impractical. A sender can't distinguish "the message was never received" from "the message was received but the ack was lost" without an additional mechanism, and that mechanism is client-side deduplication. Real systems get the user-visible experience of exactly-once by combining at-least-once delivery (retry until acknowledged, accepting duplicates) with deduplication by a client-generated, retry-stable message ID, which is simpler to implement correctly and just as effective for the user.

exercises.prompt: User A is connected to connection-server-7. Connection-server-7 crashes unexpectedly, and the connection registry entry for user A ('conn:userA' -> 'connection-server-7') has not yet been updated or expired. At this exact moment, user B sends A a message. Using a system built with store-and-forward (durable persist happens before live-delivery lookup), predict what happens to the message, and separately predict what A's client experiences when it reconnects to a new connection server a few seconds later.
exercises.code:
State at time of crash:
  connection_registry.get("conn:userA") -> "connection-server-7"  (STALE -- server 7 is down)
  B sends a message to A via connection-server-3 (B's own connection server)

send_message flow (per the store-and-forward example):
  1. message_store.append(...)   -- runs FIRST, unconditionally
  2. connection_registry.get("conn:userA") -> "connection-server-7" (stale)
  3. attempt deliver_live("connection-server-7", ...) -> fails (server 7 is down)
hints: Look at the order of operations in send_message -- does the durable persist happen before or after the live-delivery attempt, and does that ordering matter here?
The live-delivery attempt to the crashed server-7 will fail -- but does that failure roll back or undo step 1, the durable persist?
When A reconnects to a NEW connection server, how does A's client learn about messages it missed while disconnected -- via a leftover live push, or via an explicit sync request?
exercises.expectedAnswer: The message is NOT lost: step 1 (the durable persist to message_store) completed before the live-delivery attempt in step 3 ran, and step 3's failure (connection-server-7 is down) doesn't undo step 1, so the message safely exists in the durable store. When A reconnects (to a new connection server, since server 7 is gone), A's client doesn't depend on any leftover push from the crashed server. It performs a sync_on_reconnect-style request for everything in the conversation since the last message it has, which the durable store can answer correctly regardless of which connection servers have crashed or been replaced, so A sees B's message shortly after reconnecting.
exercises.solutionExplanation: This scenario is why store-and-forward orders its steps the way it does: durability is unconditional and first, so a live-delivery failure for any reason, including the recipient's whole connection server crashing, can only delay when the recipient sees the message, never lose it. The stale registry entry is a harmless side effect of the crash (it gets corrected on A's next connect, or expires after its TTL, which bounds how long the stale pointer can exist) and creates no data-loss risk, because the system never depended on the registry or the live-push path being reliable. Reconnect-time sync against the durable store is the dependable guarantee, and live push is a latency optimization for the common case where everything is healthy.

exercises.prompt: A team scales their chat backend's connection-handling tier from 1 server to 10 servers behind a load balancer, expecting straightforward horizontal scaling like any other stateless tier. After the change, users report that messages sent to them frequently 'never arrive' even though the sender's message clearly succeeded. Investigation shows each connection server tracks its own currently-connected users in a plain in-memory dict, with no shared registry. Diagnose the bug and fix it.
hints: This is structurally the exact same bug as the in-memory shopping-cart example from the load-balancing and statelessness module -- what's different here that makes the fix slightly harder than 'just move the data to Redis'?
If user A is connected to server 4, but the message is being sent from code running on server 9, does server 9's own connected_users dict have any way of knowing A is on server 4?
You need something server 9 CAN look up (which server holds A's connection), even though the actual open socket itself can't be moved into a shared store the way a shopping cart's data could be.
exercises.solutionCode:
import redis
registry = redis.Redis(host="registry.internal")

connected_users = {}  # still local -- holds the ACTUAL socket handles for THIS server only

def on_connect(user_id, websocket):
    connected_users[user_id] = websocket
    registry.set(f"conn:{user_id}", THIS_SERVER_ID, ex=60)  # shared pointer; a heartbeat must refresh it

def on_disconnect(user_id):
    del connected_users[user_id]
    registry.delete(f"conn:{user_id}")

def send_message_to_user(recipient_id, message):
    ws = connected_users.get(recipient_id)
    if ws is not None:
        ws.send(message)   # recipient is on THIS server -- deliver directly
        return
    target_server = registry.get(f"conn:{recipient_id}")
    if target_server is not None:
        forward_to_server(target_server, recipient_id, message)  # internal RPC/pub-sub
    # else: recipient is genuinely offline -- rely on store-and-forward / reconnect sync
exercises.solutionExplanation: The root cause is the same as the shopping-cart bug from the load-balancing lesson: state (here, which user is connected where) lives in one instance's private memory, so no other instance can see it. But the fix can't be the same, because what's being tracked, an open TCP socket, can't be moved into Redis the way cart data could; a socket handle is only meaningful in the process that opened it. The fix keeps the socket handles local (each server still needs its own `connected_users` dict for sockets it physically holds) and adds a shared connection registry holding a *pointer*: which server currently owns this user's connection. Any of the 10 servers, on receiving a message for a recipient it doesn't hold, can look up the target server and forward the message internally instead of dropping it. Before the fix, a message was delivered only if sender and recipient happened to be connected to the same one of the ten servers, which explains the "frequently never arrives" symptom: most pairs, spread randomly across 10 servers, weren't colocated. One detail in the code: the registry key has a 60-second expiry, so a long-lived connection needs a periodic heartbeat that refreshes it, or the entry vanishes while the user is still connected.

assessments.prompt: A chat client sends a message, and the server's acknowledgment is lost in transit due to a network blip, so the client retries by sending the same message again with the same client-generated message ID. What should a correctly-designed server do, and which delivery guarantee does this describe?
options: Reject the retried message entirely and require the user to manually resend it with a new ID.

Recognize the retry via the repeated client-generated message ID, avoid creating a duplicate, and re-send the acknowledgment -- this is at-least-once delivery combined with client-side deduplication, which produces exactly-once delivery from the user's perspective without needing true exactly-once transport semantics.
Persist and deliver the message twice, since the network layer is responsible for guaranteeing delivery, not the application.
Switch to at-most-once delivery so the retry never happens in the first place.
assessments.explanation: This is the at-least-once-plus-deduplication pattern: the client's retry is a legitimate response to a lost acknowledgment, not a new message, and because it carries the same client-generated ID as the original, the server recognizes it as a duplicate of a message it already has, skips re-persisting it, and resends the ack the client is waiting for. The “Persist and deliver the message twice, since…” option produces a visible duplicate, which is the failure deduplication prevents. The “Reject the retried message entirely and require…” option defeats the purpose of retrying and makes for an unreliable experience. The “Switch to at-most-once delivery so the retry…” option misunderstands the tradeoff: at-most-once doesn't prevent the need for retries, it refuses to perform them, trading duplicate risk for loss risk, the opposite of what chat wants.

assessments.prompt: Explain why designing a chat system is a different problem than designing a typical CRUD API, referring to the statelessness principle and the consistency-tradeoffs lesson, and describe how the design responds to each.
assessments.modelAnswer: A typical CRUD API, and even a read-heavy system like a URL shortener, fits the request/response model the earlier modules were built around: a client sends a self-contained request, a stateless server handles it using only that request plus whatever it can fetch from a shared store, and sends back a response, which lets a load balancer route across interchangeable instances and lets horizontal scaling work without correctness problems. A chat system breaks that model at its foundation: a user has to receive messages the server initiates at arbitrary moments, which requires a long-lived, open, bidirectional connection between the client and one specific server for as long as the user is online. That connection is state pinned to one machine's memory, and the socket can't be relocated to a shared store the way a shopping cart's data could, so the statelessness principle can't simply be reapplied. It has to be worked around with a connection registry that tracks which server holds which user's socket, so any server delivering a message can find and forward to the right one. Consistency is the second place chat diverges. The consistency-tradeoffs lesson advises matching the guarantee to what a feature needs instead of using the strongest option everywhere, and chat is a clean case: within one conversation, both participants need a consistent ordering of messages, which takes some coordination (a per-conversation sequence number assigned at durable-write time), but there's no need for a single global ordering across every conversation, which would be extremely expensive and which users would never notice or benefit from. So the design applies strong-enough ordering narrowly, per conversation, where it's needed, and leaves everything else eventually consistent or uncoordinated: the same "match, don't maximize" instinct, applied to a different traffic shape than the read-heavy request/response systems the earlier modules mostly assumed.

assessments.prompt: Why can't the 'externalize state to a shared store' fix used for shopping carts (moving cart data into Redis) be applied directly to a user's open WebSocket connection?
options: Because WebSocket connections are always encrypted, and Redis cannot store encrypted data.
Because WebSockets are not compatible with Redis under any circumstances.

Because the actual open TCP socket itself, not just data associated with it, is pinned to one specific machine's memory and cannot be moved into a shared store -- so the registry has to hold a pointer to which server owns the connection, rather than the connection itself.
Because shopping cart data and connection data are stored in different data formats that Redis cannot represent.
assessments.explanation: Unlike a shopping cart's data, the open TCP socket itself, not just data associated with it, is pinned to one machine's memory and can't be moved, so the fix is a connection registry that doesn't hold the state itself but a pointer to which instance does. The “Because WebSockets are not compatible with Redis…” option fabricates an incompatibility that isn't the reason. The “Because shopping cart data and connection data…” option invents a data-format restriction. The “Because WebSocket connections are always encrypted…” option invents an encryption limitation.

assessments.prompt: In the store-and-forward pattern, why does the durable persist to the message store happen before the attempt at live delivery, rather than after?
options: Because the recipient's connection server needs to read the message from the store before it is allowed to accept any live connection at all.
Because durable writes are always faster to execute than live-delivery attempts, so ordering them first improves latency.
Because live delivery is only attempted for messages that fail to persist, as a fallback mechanism.
Because durability is the actual guarantee the system provides.
assessments.explanation: Durability happens first and unconditionally, and live delivery is attempted afterward as a best-effort optimization on top of a guarantee that doesn't depend on it succeeding. If deliver_live fails, nothing is lost: the message already exists in message_store. The “Because durable writes are always faster…” option makes an unsupported latency claim. The “Because the recipient's connection server needs…” option invents a dependency on connection acceptance. The “Because live delivery is only attempted…” option inverts the relationship: live delivery is attempted after persistence regardless of outcome, not only when persistence fails.

assessments.prompt: Why is a per-conversation sequence number sufficient for ordering, with no need for a single global ordering across every conversation in the system?
options: Because per-conversation sequence numbers automatically produce a valid global ordering as a side effect, making a separate global mechanism redundant.
Because global ordering across all conversations is technically impossible to implement in any database.
Because chat systems are legally required to keep each conversation's data completely isolated from every other conversation.
Because users only need to see messages within one conversation in a consistent relative order.
assessments.explanation: There's no need for a single global ordering across every conversation: that would demand an expensive, coordinated, strongly consistent write path of the kind the consistency-tradeoffs lesson warned against reaching for by default, and users only need messages within one conversation in a consistent order. The “Because global ordering across all conversations…” option overstates the claim: global ordering isn't impossible, only unnecessary and expensive. The “Because chat systems are legally required…” option invents a legal requirement. The “Because per-conversation sequence numbers automatically produce…” option is false: per-conversation numbers say nothing about order across conversations, and no global ordering falls out as a side effect.

assessments.prompt: What makes a chat system break the stateless request/response assumption that earlier modules in this subject relied on?
options: Chat messages are too large to fit in a typical HTTP request body, forcing a different transport.

A user needs to receive messages the server initiates at any moment, with no client request for that message to be a response to -- which requires a long-lived, open, bidirectional connection tied to one specific machine, reintroducing exactly the statefulness the earlier modules worked to design away from.
Chat systems cannot use a database at all, unlike the request/response systems covered earlier.
Chat systems use a different network protocol (WebSockets) that happens to be incompatible with load balancers.
assessments.explanation: A user needs to receive messages the server initiates at any moment, with no client request for the message to be a response to. That requires a long-lived, open, bidirectional connection, which is state tied to one specific machine. The “Chat systems use a different network protocol…” option misattributes the issue to load-balancer incompatibility; load balancers can still assign initial connections, and the problem is what happens after. The “Chat messages are too large to fit…” option invents a size limit. The “Chat systems cannot use a database…” option is contradicted by the store-and-forward design, which depends on a durable database.
